title: The spire at Pandharpur
hook: the walk is over, the line to the god stretches out of sight, and some pilgrims bow to the temple's spire and turn for home
carry: even a bow to the spire is darshan
tomorrow: how do you beat a demon who hides under water?

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti belongs to everyone, even at the grindstone: Janabai singing before dawn, and Vitthal taking the handle.

After all those days of walking, the town comes into view: Pandharpur, on the bank of the river. The singing gets louder, not softer. Then the walkers see the line to stand before Vitthal. It winds through the streets and out of sight. Some will wait in it for many hours. And some, the story of the road says, walk down to the river, bathe, look up at the temple's spire, bow, and turn for home, content. So was the whole walk wasted, for the ones who never reach his feet?
screen: `PANDHARPUR COMES INTO VIEW.` → `A LINE OUT OF SIGHT.` → `A BOW TO THE SPIRE.`

segments.voice: The river at Pandharpur is the Bhima, and here Varkaris call it the Chandrabhaga, because, tradition says, it bends like a crescent moon. Pilgrims bathe in it first. On the holy day itself, the Ekadashi, the crowd reaches its peak. Inside the temple, Vitthal stands on his brick, hands on hips, the way Pundalik left him, and pilgrims are allowed close enough to lay their heads on his feet. A child running to a mother doesn't stop at arm's length. But the line is long, and not everyone reaches the feet. So Varkari tradition holds that seeing the kalas, the temple's pinnacle, from outside is darshan too. Darshan is one of the plainest acts of Hindu worship: you go to see God, and, just as much, to be seen by God. And in the Varkari songs, Vitthal is the one who waits: he stood on that brick for Pundalik and never left. Many teachers read it this way: a God who is waiting is already looking at you, whether you're at his feet or on the riverbank. Then the walkers go home, to fields and shops and kitchens, until the next wari. And it's why, at any temple, someone who can't manage the line may fold their hands toward the spire from outside, and mean it. The walk wasn't wasted. They were seen.
screen: `A BATH IN THE CHANDRABHAGA` · `A HEAD ON VITTHAL'S FEET` · `DARSHAN: TO SEE AND BE SEEN` · `THE SPIRE COUNTS TOO`

segments.voice: Find one image that's holy to you, a picture of a god on a shelf, a temple you love, or just the sky through a window, and look at it the way pilgrims look up at the spire: steadily, hands folded if you like. For a few breaths, let yourself be looked at back. If you don't pray, rest your eyes on something you love and let seeing it from where you are be enough.
Maharashtra's Varkari. The walkers who reach Pandharpur, bow at Vitthal's feet or to his spire, and go home until the next wari. Today's word.
Carry this: even a bow to the spire is darshan. You're seen from where you stand. Until tomorrow, far north, in Kashmir.
